value.overview: The Elegant Tern is a slender, ocean-going seabird of the eastern Pacific. It is recognizable by its long, narrow orange bill, shaggy black crest, pointed wings, and deeply forked tail. Most of the population breeds in a small number of dense colonies in northwestern Mexico, especially the Gulf of California, with some colonies in coastal California. After breeding, birds disperse along the Pacific coast and offshore waters in search of small schooling fish.
value.classification: The Elegant Tern belongs to the tern family Laridae and the order Charadriiformes. Its scientific name is Thalasseus elegans.
value.identification: This medium-sized tern measures about 39–42 cm long. Adults have pale gray upperparts, white underparts, long pointed wings, a forked tail, dark legs, and a long, slender orange to reddish-orange bill that often droops slightly at the tip. Breeding adults show a shaggy black crest and may have a faint pink wash below. Nonbreeding adults have a whiter forehead. Juveniles are more heavily patterned and have duller, yellower bills.
value.rangeHabitat: Elegant Terns breed mainly on sandy islands, beaches, and low coastal islands in northwestern Mexico, particularly in the Gulf of California, with smaller breeding colonies in southern and central California. Outside the breeding season they use coastal waters, bays, estuaries, beaches, and nearshore marine habitats along the Pacific coast of North and South America. In Costa Rica, the species is a rare or occasional visitor, recorded mainly along the Pacific coast; it is not known to breed there.
value.migrationStatus: Partly migratory and highly dispersive. After breeding, many birds move north along the California coast, while others disperse south through Pacific coastal waters toward Central and South America. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon migrant or nonbreeding visitor on the Pacific coast rather than a regular resident. Numbers and timing may vary with food supply and ocean conditions such as El Niño.
value.breeding: Elegant Terns nest in dense colonies on open, sparsely vegetated ground, including sandy islands and beaches. The nest is usually a shallow scrape in the soil. Both adults participate in courtship, incubation, and care of the young. Colonies may occur with other terns or protective gull species, which can help deter predators. Chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and gather in groups while adults continue bringing them fish.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on small schooling fish, especially northern anchovies where those fish are abundant. It may also take sardines, silversides, gobies, mackerel, and some small crustaceans. An Elegant Tern typically searches while flying low over the sea, briefly hovering before plunging into the water to seize prey. It often forages close to shore and may gather in mixed flocks with other seabirds.
value.behavior: Elegant Terns are active, social seabirds that commonly rest and roost in large groups on beaches, rocky islets, sandbars, pilings, and other coastal structures. They are agile fliers and frequently forage in flocks. During the breeding season they defend dense colonies with loud calls and coordinated aerial activity. Their movements and breeding success can change substantially as oceanographic conditions affect the abundance and distribution of schooling fish.

conservation.populationTrend: The long-term population trend is considered declining, although numbers fluctuate considerably between years in response to anchovy availability, oceanographic conditions, and other environmental pressures. Some colonies in California have expanded, while the species has declined or disappeared from certain former breeding sites in western Mexico.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include concentration of the breeding population at a few vulnerable colonies, disturbance by people and low-flying aircraft or drones, predation and competition at nesting sites, reduced availability of anchovies and other prey, fisheries interactions, pollution, and climate-driven changes in marine productivity. Storms, flooding, and other events can also cause substantial losses at colonies.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and carefully manage breeding islands, beaches, estuaries, and important roosts. Keep people, pets, boats, drones, and aircraft away from nesting colonies and follow seasonal access restrictions. Support sustainable fisheries and marine protected areas that conserve forage fish and feeding habitat. In Costa Rica, report sightings through established bird-monitoring programs and avoid disturbing uncommon terns resting or feeding along the Pacific coast.
